title: Vision
text:
Ecologists routinely investigate why populations change, species interact, communities assemble, and ecosystems respond to disturbance. Their studies contribute observations, experiments, statistical estimates, predictions, and explanations. But synthesizing these contributions as causal knowledge is more demanding than collecting the relationships they report.
Studies can examine similarly named variables yet address different interventions, outcomes, populations, timescales, or causal pathways. Even when authors use comparable causal language, the assumptions supporting their interpretations may differ. An apparent consensus in reported associations need not constitute agreement about an identifiable causal effect.

title: Vision
section: A missing dimension in the literature
text:
A missing dimension in the literature
Conventional reviews and literature-mining systems are valuable for organizing topics, methods, variables, and conclusions. The Causal Atlas of Ecology asks what additional understanding becomes possible when we also attend to the causal question a study poses, the assumptions its inference requires, and the evidence it provides.
This is not a claim that existing ecological studies lack value. Rather, it is an invitation to examine more carefully which kinds of knowledge each study contributes, where uncertainty remains, and when findings are meaningfully comparable.

title: Vision
text:
Our long-term vision
The program aims to develop systematic, reproducible approaches for interpreting and evaluating causal knowledge in published ecological research. Over time, validated methods could support structured representations of causal questions, assumptions, and evidence, enabling new kinds of comparison and synthesis across studies.




Three-stage conceptual vision: published research, reconstruction and evaluation, structured causal knowledge.



Long-term research vision. The diagram illustrates conceptual stages, not an implemented end-to-end system.

title: Vision
text:
Why begin with ecology?
Ecological systems are complex, interconnected, and dynamic. Their study combines experiments, observations, longitudinal measurements, comparative designs, and models across scales. Ecologists also confront familiar inferential challenges: confounding, feedback, imperfect measurement, selection, and context-dependent effects.
These characteristics make ecology an especially informative setting for investigating the relationship between scientific questions, causal assumptions, analytical decisions, and conclusions.

title: Vision
text:
Potential beyond ecology
Although ecology is the program’s initial focus, the underlying questions are relevant to many disciplines that attempt to infer causes from heterogeneous bodies of evidence. Any extension beyond ecology would require domain-specific evaluation, methodological adaptation, and independent validation.

Scope note. The Atlas is a research program, not presently a complete database of ecological causal relationships. Its long-term form will depend on what the development and validation phases establish.

title: Are we answering the question we asked?
text: A study can fit a sophisticated statistical model, obtain precise coefficients, and still leave its central scientific question unresolved. The issue is not necessarily poor modeling. It may be a mismatch between the question that motivated the work and the quantity the analysis actually estimates.

title: Are we answering the question we asked?
text:
From question to target
Suppose an ecologist asks about the total effect of canopy cover on bird abundance. That question differs from asking about a direct effect that excludes changes through food resources, or about the association between canopy cover and bird counts among otherwise similar sampled sites. Each quantity can be scientifically useful, but they are not interchangeable.
A target causal quantity, or estimand, clarifies what is being compared. A causal model can then help identify the assumptions needed to connect the target to observed data. Only after that step does it make sense to debate an estimator, functional form, or model-fitting procedure.

title: Are we answering the question we asked?
text:
Models are tools, not questions
Generalized linear models, mixed models, additive models, and structural equation models can each serve important roles. None independently defines the scientific effect of interest. Adding covariates, selecting paths, or optimizing fit cannot substitute for deciding which effect the study intends to learn.
The practical lesson is not to abandon familiar models. It is to organize their use around clearly specified questions and assumptions.

title: Are we answering the question we asked?
text:
A question for readers
Could two analysts fit the same dataset successfully while answering different causal questions? If so, what would you need to specify before deciding which result is relevant?
Return to Perspectives

title: Causal language is not causal identification
text: Ecologists often write that one factor drives, determines, shapes, or influences another. These words can express a scientific hypothesis, summarize a proposed mechanism, or interpret an empirical result. But their causal force does not, by itself, establish that the study design and analysis identify the effect being discussed.

title: Causal language is not causal identification
text:
A distinction worth preserving
Consider a study reporting that forest cover is associated with bird abundance. A causal question might ask how bird abundance would change if forest cover were altered, holding relevant background conditions appropriately in view. That intervention-oriented question is not answered merely by finding a statistical association. It also requires assumptions about possible common causes, measurement, selection, and the temporal organization of the system.
A paper may be careful in its methods but expansive in its discussion. Another may pose a causal question in its introduction yet report only predictive performance. Neither pattern can be judged adequately by counting a few words in isolation. The scientific meaning depends on the relationship among the question, evidence, analysis, and interpretation.

title: Causal language is not causal identification
text:
Why it matters for synthesis
If a review treats every causal-sounding statement as an identified causal finding, it risks combining conclusions that have different evidentiary status. Conversely, treating all observational findings as merely descriptive can obscure important design-based causal work. A more useful approach is to evaluate the claims and their inferential support separately.
The Causal Atlas of Ecology investigates how such distinctions can be made systematically across scientific literature. That remains a research question, not a completed census of ecological practice.

title: Causal language is not causal identification
text:
A question for readers
When you read that a variable affects an outcome, can you identify the intervention, comparison, population, and assumptions that give that statement its causal meaning?
Return to Perspectives

title: Development
text: The Causal Atlas of Ecology is being developed as a sequence of research phases. The roadmap describes the intended progression of work, not a set of completed deliverables or fixed launch commitments. Methods and priorities may change in response to pilot evaluation, expert review, and available resources.

title: Development
text:
Research roadmap


Phase I · Foundational research


Conceptual foundations
Clarify the relationships among causal questions, scientific claims, assumptions, estimands, identification, and evidence synthesis. Establish the conceptual distinctions that guide subsequent analysis.
Intended output: A coherent research framework and initial methodological principles.




Phase II · Methods development


Protocols and reference evaluation
Develop systematic procedures for interpreting and assessing causal information in scientific publications, alongside strategies for expert evaluation and reproducibility.
Intended output: Research protocols and evaluation approaches suitable for pilot testing.




Phase III · Pilot research


Testing and validation
Investigate the consistency, interpretability, limitations, and reliability of proposed analytical methods. Use the findings to refine the framework and identify where human expertise remains essential.
Intended output: Evidence about the strengths and limitations of candidate methods.




Phase IV · Broader analysis


Expansion across ecological literature
Apply sufficiently evaluated approaches to more diverse ecological studies, examine variation across research contexts, and assess the robustness of emerging patterns.
Intended output: Research analyses and manuscripts appropriate to the maturity of the evidence.




Phase V · Public research products


Atlas construction and dissemination
Explore structured synthesis products, documented methods, publications, and appropriate public resources that can support future causal research.
Intended output: Public research products whose scope is supported by prior validation.

title: Development
text:
Current focus
The program’s initial emphasis is on conceptual development and systematic approaches to evaluating published ecological studies. Protocol refinement and pilot evaluation are part of this early work. The descriptions here are deliberately qualitative; quantitative results will be reported only when appropriately checked and ready for dissemination.

Development status (October 2026). Early-stage research and methods development. The phases above are a roadmap, not a statement that all stages have started. No comprehensive public Atlas or production-scale analysis is claimed.

title: About this site
text:
This is the public-facing website of the Causal Atlas of Ecology, a developing research program of the Behavioral Complexity and Causality Lab at the University of Wyoming.
The site presents the program’s motivation, research agenda, development roadmap, and scholarly perspectives. It does not currently provide a comprehensive causal database, a validated public corpus, or a production research service.

Editorial conventions

Vision describes long-term ambitions, not completed infrastructure.
Research describes questions and principles, not confirmed empirical conclusions.
Development distinguishes planned phases from verifiable progress.
Perspectives are scholarly commentary rather than findings of the Atlas.

title: Home
text:
Scientific research program · In development




Mapping the causal knowledge embedded in ecological science.

Ecology has produced an extraordinary body of research investigating why natural systems behave as they do. Yet the causal knowledge contained in this literature remains difficult to evaluate, compare, and synthesize. Studies may share variables and terminology while asking different questions, invoking different assumptions, and supporting different inferences.
The Causal Atlas of Ecology is a developing research program investigating how ecological studies formulate causal questions, support their claims, and contribute to an accumulating body of causal knowledge.

title: Home
text:
The scientific challenge
A statistical relationship is not automatically an answer to a causal question. Nor do two reported effects necessarily describe the same causal quantity. Meaningful synthesis requires attention to what was asked, what was measured, what assumptions were made, and what the evidence can support.
The Atlas seeks to make these distinctions more explicit and, over time, more systematically examinable across the ecological literature.




Conceptual relationship among scientific questions, causal assumptions, evidence, and synthesis.



Conceptual framework: causal knowledge synthesis depends on interpreting questions, assumptions, and evidence together. This is a research vision, not a depiction of an operational atlas.

title: When evidence accumulates, does knowledge?
text: A growing literature can make a scientific topic appear well understood. Many studies may report effects involving the same variables, and a synthesis may combine their estimates into a compelling summary. Yet an important question remains: are the studies estimating the same thing?

title: When evidence accumulates, does knowledge?
text:
The challenge of comparability
Two studies may both examine how habitat disturbance relates to biodiversity, while differing in exposure definition, temporal scale, sampled populations, confounding structure, and treatment of intermediate variables. A coefficient from one analysis may represent a conditional association; another may approximate a total causal effect under explicit assumptions. Averaging them does not automatically create a meaningful causal summary.
This is not an argument against meta-analysis or evidence synthesis. It is an argument for making the inferential target and supporting assumptions part of the synthesis itself.

title: When evidence accumulates, does knowledge?
text:
Toward structured causal evidence
A richer account of scientific knowledge would describe not only which variables appear together in the literature, but also the questions researchers asked, the assumptions they relied upon, and the limits of what their designs could identify. Such structure might help reveal areas of agreement, unresolved ambiguity, and opportunities for stronger research designs.
Developing and evaluating methods for that kind of synthesis is a long-term objective of the Causal Atlas of Ecology. Its feasibility and limitations must be established through research rather than presumed in advance.

title: When evidence accumulates, does knowledge?
text:
A question for readers
Before pooling reported effects, can you explain why they represent comparable causal quantities?
Return to Perspectives

title: Research
text: The Causal Atlas of Ecology is organized around four connected lines of inquiry. They define the program’s scientific scope without presupposing the outcomes of ongoing research.

title: Research
text:
01 · Causal language and scientific claims
How do ecological papers express questions about causes, effects, and mechanisms? How does the language of a study’s motivation compare with its description of methods and its interpretation of results?
This theme examines the relationship between what a paper appears to ask and what its authors claim to have learned. It recognizes that descriptive, associational, predictive, and causal statements serve different scientific purposes.

title: Research
text:
02 · Causal identification
Under what conditions do study designs and analytical choices support the causal effects being discussed? Which assumptions are stated, which are left implicit, and which may be difficult to assess from a published account?
Identification concerns whether a causal quantity can, in principle, be learned from available evidence under a specified set of assumptions. It is distinct from choosing a statistical model or obtaining a precise estimate.




A stylized causal diagram showing a common cause, exposure, mediator, and outcome.



Illustrative causal structure. Arrows express hypothesized causal relationships, not relationships established by data. Different causal questions can require different treatment of the same variables.

title: Research
text:
03 · Causal reconstruction
Can scientific questions, proposed causal structures, and relevant inferential assumptions be reconstructed systematically from published research? How should ambiguity, missing information, and competing interpretations be represented?
This theme considers both the promise and limitations of computational assistance. A reconstructed diagram is an interpretation of reported evidence and assumptions, not independent proof of a causal structure.

title: Research
text:
04 · Causal knowledge synthesis
When do results from separate studies address comparable causal quantities? How can differences in context, measurement, population, intervention, and assumptions be made visible during synthesis?
The long-term aim is to move beyond aggregating reported relationships toward evaluating which bodies of evidence can support particular causal questions.

title: Research
text:
Methodological commitments
The program is guided by five principles:

Questions before models. State the scientific question and target causal quantity before interpreting an estimator.
Assumptions made explicit. Separate causal assumptions from statistical associations and fitted relationships.
Identification before estimation. Ask whether a target effect is identifiable before debating how precisely it can be estimated.
Uncertainty and ambiguity retained. Treat incomplete reporting and alternative interpretations as substantive limitations, not details to be silently filled in.
Evaluation and reproducibility. Subject computational procedures to expert scrutiny, documentation, and validation before making broad empirical claims.

title: Research
section: What this page does not claim
text:
What this page does not claim
These themes describe an active research agenda. They do not imply that all four lines of inquiry have been completed, that automated reconstruction is fully validated, or that the Atlas currently contains a comprehensive body of identified causal effects.
